name: North Dakota
summary_text: North Dakota stands under the United States national framework in every respect that governs a trans visitor's documents, screening and entry. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, issues new passports only as M or F according to supporting documents, and leaves previously issued X-marker passports valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed those passport restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, some left stranded abroad; the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records.  North Dakota law independently closes the document route that a trans visitor may rely on at the state level. The 2023 statute tracked by the Movement Advancement Project bans all gender marker changes on birth certificates, with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery. The tracker marks North Dakota a negative law state, and a stricter and more explicit surgical requirement than applies in many other states. A July 2026 national anti-trans legal-risk assessment built from five years of daily legislative tracking places North Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults and among the states that prohibit any changes to birth certificates, a rule that forces trans people to out themselves when showing documents. The same assessment records that federal policies continue to create legal difficulties for transgender people nationwide.  Facilities access is restricted across a growing group of states: a Movement Advancement Project tally counts bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity elsewhere, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, described by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law. Screening inside the country carries an outing risk of its own, since TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy; several foreign governments have responded, with advisories about trans people travelling to the United States issued from April 2025 and at least eight European countries adjusting entry guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens by March 2025.

name: Ohio
summary_text: Ohio is a state within the United States, so a visitor stands first under the national framework: Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to correct the application of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.  Entry screening carries an outing risk that applies at every United States port of entry, including Ohio's airports. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the country to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating an applicant who lists a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent fraud-based ban. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, and several foreign governments, including at least eight European states, adjusted travel guidance for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.  Ohio's principal own measure concerns facilities. Governor Mike DeWine signed Senate Bill 104, the Protect All Students Act, on 27 November 2024; it took effect on 25 February 2025, ninety days after signing. The statute requires every public and private K-12 school, college and university in Ohio to designate restrooms, locker rooms, changing and shower rooms and overnight accommodations for the exclusive use of males or females on the basis of sex assigned at or near birth, which in practice directs trans students to facilities matching their birth-certificate sex.  The Ohio statute contains no enforcement mechanism. It was signed out of public view and over the objections of Democrats, teachers' unions and civil-rights groups, and was sponsored by Republican state Senator Jerry Cirino.  A national legal risk assessment published 27 August 2026 places Ohio in its worst-graded group of fifteen states, a tier below the four states flagged Do Not Travel (Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas), under a national frame of worst policies in effect.  Wider national exposure remains relevant to a visitor who is detained or needs care. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy; the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as chemical and surgical mutilation of children, some hospitals paused care, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

sources.title: Ohio HB68 - Saving Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act
sources.documents: Bans gender-affirming puberty blockers, hormones, and surgery for under-18; bans transgender girls/women from women's high school and college sports teams
sources.detail: Passed Dec 13, 2023; vetoed Dec 29, 2023 by Gov. DeWine; veto overridden by House Jan 10, 2024 and Senate Jan 24, 2024; blocked April 2024, allowed Aug 2024, injunction reinstated March 18, 2025 by 10th District Court of Appeals, AG Dave Yost vowed appeal
